pages.description: H.R.131 would have reduced what communities in Colorado must repay the federal government for building the Arkansas Valley Conduit, a federal water pipeline. It would have lowered the interest they owe and extended their repayment period.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect Compared with the law on January 8, 2026, H.R.131 would ease local repayments for completing the conduit, a water pipeline.

  • Because Existing law requires “35 percent nonfederal repayment over a 50-year period, starting after project completion.” [1]
  • Because If the Interior Secretary finds financial hardship, the bill allows repayment of the remaining balance “for a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [2].
  • Because The bill also counts construction contributions toward the local share: “funding provided during construction from any entity other than the Secretary” [2].
  • Because After costs rose, the local water district testified that project revenue could no longer cover the local share on the old terms: “miscellaneous revenues were expected to be more than sufficient to repay 35 percent of the AVC’s cost with interest and within 50 years. With the May, 2024, updated cost estimate, this is no longer true. Repayment can now be accomplished only if the interest rate is reduced to at least half the current project rate and the repayment period is at least 75 years” [3].
  • Because After the veto, the district’s president placed this constraint on the later part of the line: “It’s when we get to the second half of the project where it will be challenging to build and repay our portion of the debt” [4]. He added: “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” [4]
  • Because The project replaces poor groundwater with cleaner water: “The AVC will provide a new surface water source of high quality” [3].
  • So Easing this repayment barrier helps communities finish the conduit and switch water sources, enabling the environmental benefits below.

points.title: Cleaner source water reduces polluted treatment waste that threatens rivers and aquatic life.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Cleaner source water reduces polluted treatment waste that threatens rivers and aquatic life.

  • Because Treating local groundwater creates concentrated waste: “When this groundwater is cleaned to drinking water standards, in many cases it produces a reject stream which violates EPA discharge standards.” [3]
  • Because La Junta and Las Animas use reverse osmosis, a filtering process. Their waste reaches the river: “The brine, or salty wastewater, from both towns’ reverse osmosis systems is dumped back into the Arkansas River, creating a new environmental challenge.” [5]
  • Because The waste carries harmful pollutants. An earlier report describes brine “too thick with selenium and other contaminants” [6] and says selenium “becomes damaging to both human and aquatic life at high levels.” [6]
  • Because Conduit water gives Las Animas a source needing simpler treatment: “The pipeline would deliver clean water straight to the town, requiring only standard treatment like filtration and disinfection.” [5]
  • So Helping communities make this switch reduces the need to produce and discharge polluted concentrate. Protecting rivers and aquatic life from that pollution serves [NAME]’s care for nature.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction money. In May 2025 the district reported Reclamation funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” After the veto, the district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The district president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [7], [8], [4].

Evidence note: Rocky Mountain PBS reports that under current appropriations the pipeline would not reach La Junta and Las Animas. It also reports that La Junta is applying for grants to rehabilitate its plant to reduce concentrate volume, and that Las Animas must eventually discontinue river discharge. The 2013 EIS assumed zero liquid discharge, with brine evaporated in ponds, for all alternatives, and described the present discharge as likely not allowed to continue. Sources: [5], [9].

Evidence note: The EIS reports 2 acres of permanent upland disturbance for the Comanche North conduit alternative against 50 acres for No Action, because No Action would need brine evaporation ponds for expanded reverse osmosis at La Junta and Lamar. The EIS reports about 1,200 acres of temporary upland disturbance for No Action against 2,999 to 3,228 acres with the conduit, with disturbed areas expected to reestablish within three years. EIS No Action assumes no conduit at all, which is not the same as the no-bill path. Sources: [9].

points.title: Clean tap water lets families replace bottled water, avoiding its waste, pollution, and use of resources.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Clean tap water lets families replace bottled water, avoiding its waste, pollution, and use of resources.

  • Because Poor local water quality “forces many families to rely on bottled water or expensive filtration systems” [10].
  • So Helping provide clean tap water removes the water-quality problem driving those bottled-water purchases.
  • Because A U.S. study compared water-supply methods for the same amount of drinking water: “The functional unit for the study was 1000 gallons of drinking water” [11].
  • Because Across production, use, and disposal, tap water served in reusable cups or bottles produced less waste: “With respect to life-cycle solid waste generation, tap water systems are the preferred systems.” [11]
  • Because The study also found lower emissions of gases that warm the climate: “With respect to life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions, tap water systems are the preferred systems.” [11]
  • Because Making plastic bottles uses oil and energy. The study identifies “the manufacturing of containers from non-renewable fossil based resources” [11] and finds: “Single-use bottled systems consume 11-31 times more energy than tap systems.” [11]
  • Because Packaging also uses water beyond what people drink: “Water is consumed during the material production and fabrication of containers and packaging.” [11]
  • Because The study found lower water use for tap water than for large delivered jugs (HOD) or disposable bottles: “With respect to life-cycle water use, the municipal tap systems outperform both HOD and single-use bottled systems by a considerable margin.” [11]
  • So Enabling families to replace bottles avoids packaging and the resources used to make and deliver it. The study supports lower waste, climate pollution, energy use, and extra water use from that switch. Preventing those burdens serves [NAME]’s wish to protect nature.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction money. In May 2025 the district reported Reclamation funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” After the veto, the district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The district president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [7], [8], [4].

Evidence note: In 2014 the May Valley superintendent estimated 80 percent of customers had a softener and reverse osmosis filter at home, and said people buy bottled water partly for taste. Bottled water is therefore one of several coping methods in the area. Sources: [6].

points.title: Water with fewer damaging minerals keeps pipes and appliances in use longer, reducing waste and new production.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Water with fewer damaging minerals keeps pipes and appliances in use longer, reducing waste and new production.

  • Because The 2022 assessment confirms that the revised conduit keeps the benefit of “reducing total dissolved solids concentrations in AVC Project Participants’ water supplies” [12]. This measures minerals and other substances dissolved in water.
  • Because Reclamation explains why this matters: “total dissolved solids have corrosion and scaling effects that lead to premature deterioration of distribution pipes, water treatment equipment, and household appliances.” [13] Corrosion eats away at equipment; scaling leaves mineral deposits.
  • So Reducing this cause of early damage reduces the need to discard equipment and make replacements.
  • Because EPA explains the environmental link: “Because waste prevention prolongs the lives of materials and products, it reduces the need to manufacture new goods or reprocess materials, thereby saving energy and avoiding pollution.” [14]
  • Because Using fewer new materials also protects natural resources: “By reducing the amount of raw materials that are used in manufacturing, waste prevention conserves resources such as metals, water, and petroleum.” [14]
  • So Helping deliver lower-mineral water protects nature through less discarded equipment, less demand for new materials, and less pollution from making replacements.

Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, H.R.131 would ease repayment of communities’ 35% construction share. The change extends the repayment limit “from 50 years to 75 years” [1]. For costs not paid during construction, relief requires “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. The bill allows “a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest” [2] at “50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [2].

  • Because Financing is a barrier to completion: “the project remains unfinished, primarily due to financial constraints” [15]. On January 8, the sponsor said the relief lets communities “afford their 35 percent cost share of the project that they are statutorily obligated to repay.” [10]
  • So Making that share easier to repay supports the remaining construction and eventual operation.

points.title: Further construction temporarily clears plants and disturbs their habitats.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Further construction temporarily clears plants and disturbs their habitats.

  • Because The 2022 design estimates “Total estimated pipeline construction disturbances under the Proposed Action is 2,856 acres” [12]. This is a whole-project estimate, not the area still to be built.
  • Because The original review compares this work with the supply plan expected without the conduit: “Regional pipeline construction under the No Action Alternative would temporarily disturb about 1,200 acres of upland vegetation” [9], while “Temporary upland vegetation disturbance for alternatives with AVC range from 2,999 acres for Pueblo Dam South to 3,228 acres for Pueblo Dam North” [9].
  • Because The review predicts “short-term minor effects” [12] on upland plants from pipeline construction.
  • Because Delivery routes include places where “wetlands and/or riparian vegetation occur within or adjacent to additional delivery pipeline alignments” [12]. Riparian vegetation means plants along waterways. The current review predicts “negligible effects on wetland and riparian resources” [12].
  • Because Construction also reaches “potential habitat for Colorado plant species of concern” [12]. Their presence needs surveys: “If plants are present, transplanting or other measures would be considered to minimize effects.” [12]
  • So Repayment relief supports further temporary loss of plant cover and disturbance of living habitats. Caring for plants and their habitats gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that support.

points.title: Construction can spread invasive plants into existing plant communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Construction can spread invasive plants into existing plant communities.

  • Because The environmental review warns: “Noxious weeds could potentially invade disturbed sites after construction.” [9]
  • Because These weeds are “aggressive, nonnative plants” [9] that can displace “desirable vegetation” [9].
  • Because Construction can transport their seeds. The project’s controls include: “Cover haul trucks bringing fill materials to prevent seed transport.” [13]
  • So Financing further work supports a source of invasive-plant risk. Protecting existing plant communities gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.

Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction money. In May 2025 the district reported Reclamation funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” After the veto, the district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The district president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [7], [8], [4].

The EIS lists air quality and hazardous materials among resources with minimal effects and says weed spread would be minimized through best management practices. Sources: [13], [9].

points.title: Construction puts wild animals at risk of disturbance and death.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Construction puts wild animals at risk of disturbance and death.

  • Because The original review identifies a direct risk to sensitive reptiles: “Individual roundtail horned lizards and common kingsnakes could be killed by construction activities under all alternatives.” [9]
  • Because The 2022 review identifies possible construction effects near Cheraw Lake on “a known concentration of wintering bald eagles in that area” [12].
  • Because It also identifies an active eagle nest near the Eads spur, where “construction activities may be within 1/2 a mile of the active nest.” [12] That spur is later work: the review’s tentative schedules “estimate construction of the Eads Spur will not occur until around 2032.” [12]
  • Because The review expects these bird effects to stay small with precautions: “Proposed Action effects on bald eagles, other raptors and migratory birds would be negligible as a result of best management practices” [12].
  • So Relief supports further work that can disturb birds and kill individual reptiles. Caring for wild animals gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that support.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction money. In May 2025 the district reported Reclamation funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” After the veto, the district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The district president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [7], [8], [4].

Evidence note: The EIS says both reptiles “could be killed by construction activities under all alternatives” and describes “minor effects” on their habitat. It places roundtail horned lizard effects in regional systems under No Action and Master Contract Only and in the Pueblo Dam South and Comanche North alternatives, and common kingsnake habitat effects in pipelines near La Junta under all alternatives. Table 4-46 lists both species’ acreage as unknown, so that table does not compare reptile risk by alternative. EIS No Action is not the same as the no-bill path. Sources: [9], [13].

points.title: Operation takes water out of the river channel and worsens conditions in natural waters.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Operation takes water out of the river channel and worsens conditions in natural waters.

  • Because The 2022 review says both pipeline designs “generally decrease streamflow in the Arkansas River” [12]. They convey water in the pipe instead of the river below Pueblo Reservoir.
  • Because The original review predicts “negligible to minor increases in total dissolved solids concentrations through Pueblo” [9] and “negligible to minor adverse effects on water quality caused by increasing selenium concentrations” [9]. Total dissolved solids means dissolved salts and minerals.
  • Because The updated review retains “negligible to minor adverse effects of AVC Project on aquatic resources and water quality” [12].
  • So Supporting completion supports reduced river flow and harm to water quality and aquatic life. Protecting rivers gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that support.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction money. In May 2025 the district reported Reclamation funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” After the veto, the district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The district president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [7], [8], [4].

Evidence note: The ROD passage the PRO quotes continues that the negligible to minor adverse effects “would be too small to be detected by a monitoring program.” The EA estimates simulated deliveries at about 10,300 acre-feet a year, about 2 percent of average annual flow at the above-Pueblo gauge. Both designs include a commitment to limit excess capacity contract operations when flow is under 50 cfs at that gauge. The EIS notes occasional moderate TDS increases in dry years. Sources: [12], [9].

points.title: Changes in pumping and irrigation send more salt from groundwater into the river in summer.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Changes in pumping and irrigation send more salt from groundwater into the river in summer.

  • Because The original review attributes “minor increases to salt loading in summer months” [9] from groundwater into the Arkansas River to changes in municipal pumping and farmland irrigation.
  • Because The 2022 review keeps the earlier groundwater findings: “No changes to the AVC Project are being proposed that would result in additional effects to groundwater resources.” [12]
  • So Repayment relief supports completion and the resulting increase in salt entering the river. Protecting natural waters from this added salt gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.

In May 2025 the district reported Reclamation funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” After the veto, the district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The district president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [7], [8], [4].

points.title: Earthwork creates a risk of soil washing into waterways and damaging aquatic habitat.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Earthwork creates a risk of soil washing into waterways and damaging aquatic habitat.

  • Because The project needs “erosion control measures to prevent or reduce erosion, soil loss, and nonpoint source pollution” [13]. This means pollution washed off the work site.
  • Because Its controls aim “to minimize sedimentation and turbidity effects as a result of construction activities” [13]—soil settling in water and making it cloudy.
  • Because EPA explains the harm: “excess sediment can quickly fill rivers and lakes, requiring dredging and destroying aquatic habitats.” [16]
  • So Relief supports further earthwork that creates this runoff risk. Protecting waterways and aquatic habitats gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.

Point 7 Construction exposes the environment to fuel and oil spill risks.

  • Because The project’s spill plan addresses “any inadvertent spills of fuel, oil, hydraulic fluid, or other hazardous material during construction” [9].
  • Because Equipment care is required “to avoid or minimize contamination from automotive fluids” [13].
  • So Repayment relief supports further work involving these pollution risks. [NAME]’s wish to protect the environment from pollution gives a reason to oppose it.

Point 8 Earthwork adds dust pollution to the air.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.131 would ease repayment of the unpaid part of the communities’ construction share. It allows, “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary, repayment of the balance not covered under subparagraph (A) for a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury” [1]. Current law requires repayment “within fifty years from the time the works are first available for the delivery of water” [2]. The local share remains 35%: “payment in an amount equal to 35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [1].

points.title: It would help protect rural residents and improve their opportunities by making safe, reliable water easier to obtain.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It would help protect rural residents and improve their opportunities by making safe, reliable water easier to obtain.

  • Because Repayment costs block completion: “the project is still not completed largely because the communities that it will serve do not have the financial capacity to meet the traditional repayment obligations.” [3]
  • Because The bill addresses that barrier: “This bill would revise certain repayment terms to provide additional flexibility for local stakeholders to help finance the project and begin delivering clean, reliable water to rural communities.” [4]
  • So Easier repayment would help communities finish the pipeline and obtain a dependable water supply.
  • Because Current water sources pose a threat: “The drinking water sources they rely on are often contaminated with unsafe levels of radium, uranium, and other pollutants.” [3]
  • Because Radioactive substances in water threaten health. EPA explains: “Exposure to radionuclides from drinking water results in the increased risk of cancer.” [5] It also identifies “damage to the kidneys from exposure to the uranium itself” [5].
  • Because The pipeline would bring water safe to drink: “The AVC is designed to provide potable water from Pueblo Reservoir to 39 communities in southeastern Colorado” [3].
  • So Helping replace contaminated sources protects people whose communities lack the money to solve this problem under the usual repayment terms.
  • Because Families also bear the cost of coping with contamination: “Treating these contaminants places a significant burden on rural communities and forces many families to rely on bottled water or expensive filtration systems to meet basic needs that we all take for granted.” [3]
  • So Access to safe tap water would reduce reliance on costly alternatives and make meeting basic daily needs easier.
  • Because Schools and hospitals would receive water: “The completion of the Arkansas Valley Conduit would mean water for rural schools in communities such as Lamar, which are teaching the next generation. It would mean water for hospitals in towns such as La Junta, which are keeping Coloradans healthy.” [6]
  • Because Reliable clean water supports health, learning, and livelihoods. Reclamation calls it “an essential human need that is critical to the public health, well-being, educational attainment, and economic development of all communities in the United States.” [7]
  • So Helping supply homes, schools, hospitals, and businesses protects vulnerable residents and gives rural people basic conditions needed to learn and earn a living. Making those conditions less dependent on a community’s wealth or location advances equal opportunities.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Existing law provides 100 percent federal construction financing and 35 percent nonfederal repayment over 50 years starting after completion. H.R.131 provides no construction funds. In May 2025 the district reported funds enough to build the trunk line to Manzanola by 2030, with completion dependent on future appropriations or infrastructure funding. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected. The district president said “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [2], [8], [9], [10].

points.title: It would direct financial relief toward communities struggling to pay for a basic need.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It would direct financial relief toward communities struggling to pay for a basic need.

  • Because These communities face both rising costs and a weak economy: “families and communities across the Lower Arkansas Valley face rising water treatment costs in a declining local economy.” [7]
  • Because The bill eases the construction repayment burden by “cutting local costs by lowering the interest rate and providing more flexible repayment terms.” [11]
  • Because The easier terms depend on need: “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [1].
  • So A lower interest rate and more time to repay would ease annual pressure on local water budgets. Directing this help to communities in hardship protects people with fewer resources and treats their need for water as worthy of support despite their limited ability to pay.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District is the repayment entity. Revenue from other users of the wider project is credited toward conduit cost. Participants separately fund connection improvements, including disinfection, and the contracting parties retain care, operation, maintenance and replacement. Sources: [12], [13].

points.title: It would support economic opportunities during construction in an area with limited resources.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It would support economic opportunities during construction in an area with limited resources.

  • Because The bill helps finance construction by “easing the repayment requirements for project beneficiaries” [3].
  • Because The project plan identifies a benefit from building the pipeline itself: “Completion of the AVC is expected to boost economic activity in an economically challenged area of rural Colorado. Both through temporary impacts of construction activities as well as perpetual impacts from access to safe drinking water.” [14]
  • So Helping construction proceed supports work and business activity in a struggling rural economy. Expanding ways to earn a living in such an area advances equal opportunities.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Existing law provides 100 percent federal construction financing and 35 percent nonfederal repayment over 50 years starting after completion. H.R.131 provides no construction funds. In May 2025 the district reported funds enough to build the trunk line to Manzanola by 2030, with completion dependent on future appropriations or infrastructure funding. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected. The district president said “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [2], [8], [9], [10].

points.title: It would help honor a public commitment on which rural communities have relied.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It would help honor a public commitment on which rural communities have relied.

  • Because The commitment became law: “In 1962, President John F. Kennedy signed the Fryingpan- Arkansas Project Act (P.L. 87-590) into law.” [2] Its authorized works included the conduit: “The authorized infrastructure included the Arkansas Valley Conduit (AVC)” [2].
  • Because Communities have relied on that commitment: “it would fulfill a decades--many decades--old promise on which they have relied.” [11]
  • Because Easier repayment helps carry out the commitment: H.R.131 “facilitates the construction of the Arkansas Valley Conduit, or AVC, by easing the repayment requirements for project beneficiaries.” [3]
  • So Helping deliver a promised basic service respects the communities’ reliance. Keeping such public commitments is part of treating people justly, including people [NAME] does not know.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Existing law provides 100 percent federal construction financing and 35 percent nonfederal repayment over 50 years starting after completion. H.R.131 provides no construction funds. In May 2025 the district reported funds enough to build the trunk line to Manzanola by 2030, with completion dependent on future appropriations or infrastructure funding. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected. The district president said “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Sources: [2], [8], [9], [10].

Evidence note: The 1962 Act authorized the project and made a repayment contract a condition precedent to construction. Congress reduced the conduit’s required share to 35 percent in 2009. Reclamation’s 2024 testimony says completing the conduit “fulfills a commitment the federal government made decades ago.” H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. The 1962 repayment clause runs “as rapidly as is consistent with the contracting parties' ability to pay, but in any event, within fifty years.” Senator Bennet says Kennedy “famously promised to build” the conduit, and the Project Management Plan says completion “will fulfill a project authorization from 1962.” The text of the 1962 Pueblo address is not in the record. Sources: [15], [7], [2], [11], [14].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.131 makes federal financing for this project cheaper and longer. Current law requires “35 percent nonfederal repayment over a 50-year period” [2]. The bill keeps the 35% share but changes repayment of the balance left after construction contributions. After “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [1], it allows repayment “for a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [1].

points.title: It uses shared public resources for added financing relief while vulnerable families elsewhere still lack affordable water.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It uses shared public resources for added financing relief while vulnerable families elsewhere still lack affordable water.

  • Because Existing law bases interest on what the Treasury pays to borrow money: “the computed average interest rate payable by the Treasury upon its outstanding marketable public obligations” [2].
  • Because Financing federal water projects costs the government money. Congress’s auditors explain: “These funds are borrowed from the U.S. Treasury and accrue interest until repaid.” [16]
  • So The bill charges half that rate on the same unpaid balance and lets public financing last longer. Taxpayers cover more of the cost of lending.
  • Because Later repayment also has a cost. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) explains that an amount received “today is more valuable than the same amount received or paid in the future.” [17]
  • Because CBO lists an “Increase” [18] in direct spending of less than “$500K” [18] for the amended bill.
  • Because Other water needs remain unmet. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports that “the need for both capital investment and operations support still outpaces the tools at utilities’ disposal.” [19]
  • Because Those needs affect families’ protection and opportunities: “High water bills can force families to cut back on other essential expenses, such as food, healthcare, and education.” [19]
  • So The public resources used to cover this added financing subsidy cannot also meet other needs. Protecting vulnerable people gives [NAME] a reason to oppose having taxpayers cover these added costs while families elsewhere struggle to afford basic necessities.
  • Note The sponsor’s statement that the bill “does not authorize any additional Federal funding” [3] does not remove the cost of cheaper financing and later repayment of public money.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats the old schedule’s higher payments as money available for other needs, but the repayment district reports that those payments are in doubt. This response does not dispute that cheaper financing costs the government something, and it does not reach the PRO’s reasoning that public money covering that cost cannot also meet other needs.

  • Because The district responsible for repayment says expected project revenues no longer cover the old terms: “When Public Law 111-11 was enacted, miscellaneous revenues were expected to be more than sufficient to repay 35 percent of the AVC’s cost with interest and within 50 years. With the May, 2024, updated cost estimate, this is no longer true.” [20]
  • So The old schedule’s higher required payments cannot simply be counted as money that rejecting H.R.131 would free for other needs.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: District testimony reports a median household income of $47,000 in the conduit service area against $89,000 for Colorado. The people the relief is meant to help are themselves low-income relative to the state. Sources: [20].

Evidence note: EPA supports the water-loan program the PRO cites with “annual capitalization grants from EPA,” and H.R.131 does not change those grants. CBO’s “Increase by Less Than $500K” does not identify an affected program, and no source in the record traces this bill’s cost to a specific water-aid program. Sources: [21], [18].

points.title: It reserves new hardship relief for one project instead of giving other vulnerable communities a chance to qualify by need.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It reserves new hardship relief for one project instead of giving other vulnerable communities a chance to qualify by need.

  • Because The new terms apply to “the contract for the Arkansas Valley Conduit” [1]. Hardship outside that project cannot qualify a community for this relief.
  • Because Other communities need affordable water infrastructure. EPA reports of Martin County, Kentucky: “Failing and aging drinking water infrastructure is the main contributor to these financial challenges.” [19]
  • Because Many residents have low incomes and lack local help with bills: “Martin County is not able to support a local Customer Assistance Program because of its small population size and high percentage of low-income customers.” [19]
  • Because The problem threatens basic access: “In 2023, there were 349 residential water disconnections for nonpayment – about one in ten households.” [19]
  • Because Existing water aid does not guarantee affordable projects. EPA reports: “Subsidized DWSRF assistance offered may still not be sufficient to make projects affordable for communities.” [22] DWSRF is the federal program that helps states finance drinking-water projects.
  • Because A way to compare needs already exists. That program gives priority to projects that “assist systems most in need, on a per household basis, according to State determined affordability criteria.” [21]
  • Because Just treatment calls for people with the same basic water needs to have a chance at hardship relief based on those needs, wherever they live.
  • So The bill makes access to its added relief depend on being served by a named project. It gives other vulnerable communities no chance to have their need considered for those terms. Equal opportunities and just treatment give [NAME] a reason to oppose that unequal access to help with a basic necessity.
points.con_html:
Response Exclusion from one project’s repayment terms does not by itself show unfair access to help with the same basic water needs.

  • Because This bill changes a particular repayment duty. Reclamation explains that rising costs left the project’s beneficiaries “again faced with challenges to repay their share of construction of the project” [7].
  • Because The bill keeps payment of “35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [1] and requires “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [1] for the new repayment terms.
  • So The project boundary identifies the debt being changed; the hardship rule ties the change to difficulty paying that debt. The PRO must show why this targeted response to a repayment barrier gives people with comparable needs an unfair advantage.
  • Because Other water aid uses different forms of help. EPA says drinking-water loans “may be offered with principal forgiveness, grants, negative interest rates, or other loan forgiveness.” [21] Its program gives priority to projects that “assist systems most in need, on a per household basis, according to State determined affordability criteria.” [21]
  • Because Equal opportunities in life and just treatment concern the help people can obtain for their needs and the costs they must still bear. Eligibility for the same loan terms cannot measure that across loans, grants and forgiven debt.
  • Because EPA warns that this aid “may still not be sufficient to make projects affordable for communities.” [22] Its Martin County examples also establish unmet need. They do not compare that need, the aid available and the remaining costs with those of the Conduit communities.
  • So The PRO has not shown that H.R.131 gives an unfair preference among equally needy people. Its evidence of inadequate help elsewhere does not turn relief from this separate repayment duty into unjust treatment.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: District testimony reports a median household income of $47,000 in the conduit service area against $89,000 for Colorado. The people the relief is meant to help are themselves low-income relative to the state. Sources: [20].

Evidence note: Reclamation testified that the conduit is “unique within Reclamation’s authorized projects” in keeping repayment of a large upfront cost while serving only municipal and industrial purposes. GAO reported in 1996 that reclamation law does not require irrigators to pay interest on their repayment obligations. EPA says DWSRF loans typically run 30 years, up to 40 for disadvantaged communities, and may include principal forgiveness, grants or negative interest rates. Sources: [7], [16], [21].

pages.bill_title: the Finish the Arkansas Valley Conduit Act
statements: to be tolerant toward all kinds of people and groups
to listen to and understand people who are different to them
to accept people even when they disagree with them
pages.description: H.R.131 would have reduced what communities in Colorado must repay the federal government for building the Arkansas Valley Conduit, a federal water pipeline. It would have lowered the interest they owe and extended their repayment period.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on January 8, 2026, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, H.R.131 would ease repayment of the local and state construction share of the Arkansas Valley Conduit, a drinking-water pipeline. Existing law required “35 percent nonfederal repayment over a 50-year period, starting after project completion.” [1] With “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2], the bill allows repayment of the unpaid balance “for a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury” [2]. This would help communities “finance the project and begin delivering clean, reliable water to rural communities” [3].

points.title: It makes rural communities' own account of their needs count in the repayment rules.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It makes rural communities' own account of their needs count in the repayment rules.

  • Because Prowers County commissioners describe a funding problem: “Rural water providers in our area often struggle to secure the funding needed to meet the needs of the communities they serve.” [4]
  • Because The local water district helped draft the bill. Boebert said, “I thank the Bureau of Reclamation and the Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District for working with us in drafting this critical legislation.” [3]
  • Because The repayment burden is a barrier to finishing the pipeline: “the project is still not completed largely because the communities that it will serve do not have the financial capacity to meet the traditional repayment obligations” [5].
  • Because [NAME]'s commitment to listening to and understanding different people gives weight to a community's own account of the barriers it faces.
  • So The bill changes the payment terms in response to a barrier these communities describe and helped address. Favoring that response puts understanding of their circumstances into practice.
points.con_html:
Response Understanding the residents' funding problem does not give their proposed remedy extra weight under tolerance.

  • Because Local commissioners report a funding problem: “Rural water providers in our area often struggle to secure the funding needed to meet the needs of the communities they serve.” [4]
  • Because Boebert credits the local water district and the Bureau of Reclamation “for working with us in drafting this critical legislation” [3].
  • Because The bill bases repayment relief on “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2].
  • Because Listening gives residents' account a fair hearing. Choosing to ease their payments adds a separate goal: meeting the need they describe. Understanding a need and wanting to meet it are different aims.
  • So The PRO shows a payment change informed by local concerns. Its step from understanding those concerns to favoring relief relies on the added aim of improving water access. Calling relief a response to residents does not make that aim part of tolerance.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Boebert’s drafting credit names the Bureau of Reclamation and the district. Huffman’s “looked past their political differences” refers to House members’ treatment of the bill’s sponsors. The record does not describe how the residents differ from, or disagree with, a given reader. Sources: [3], [5].

points.title: It helps residents without requiring agreement with their politics or their representatives.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps residents without requiring agreement with their politics or their representatives.

  • Because The relief serves households' water needs. The bill's stated purpose is “To provide domestic water supplies to communities and households that do not have reliable access to domestic water supplies” [2].
  • Because Completing the project would meet that need across the communities it serves: “Once completed, the Arkansas Valley Conduit will deliver clean water to over 50,000 people in 39 rural communities across southeastern Colorado.” [6]
  • Because There is an explicit example of support across disagreement. Huffman said House members “looked past their political differences” [5] to pass this water bill.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to support useful help for them without making shared political views a condition.
  • So Favoring the repayment relief puts that acceptance into practice for these residents, whatever [NAME] thinks of their views or those of the bill's sponsors.
points.con_html:
Response Setting political dislike aside when judging aid does not turn the aid's usefulness into a reason grounded in tolerance.

  • Because The bill states a water-supply goal: “To provide domestic water supplies to communities and households that do not have reliable access to domestic water supplies” [2].
  • Because The value framework distinguishes tolerance's “Acceptance and understanding of those who are different” [7] from concern's “Commitment to equality, justice and protection” [7]. A benefit to people's welfare alone does not establish a link to accepting different people.
  • Because Huffman's example concerns setting aside the sponsors' politics: “could care less about Ms. Boebert's politics or Mr. Hurd's politics” [5].
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement rules out discounting their needs because of their views. Removing that unfair ground for opposing aid does not supply a positive reason to favor its payment terms.
  • So Huffman's example supports judging the bill without partisan bias. The PRO turns that rule for judging a policy into support for the policy's water benefit. It has not shown why this financial help itself expresses acceptance of residents across disagreement.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Boebert’s drafting credit names the Bureau of Reclamation and the district. Huffman’s “looked past their political differences” refers to House members’ treatment of the bill’s sponsors. The record does not describe how the residents differ from, or disagree with, a given reader. Sources: [3], [5].

points.title: It enacts payment terms shaped by taking opposing views seriously.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It enacts payment terms shaped by taking opposing views seriously.

  • Because Lawmakers objected to the original terms. Huffman explained that “Representative Boebert's bill did raise some concerns about removing interest payments and extending the repayment period” [5], and that “our colleagues in the Senate worked to address these shared concerns” [5].
  • Because The final bill pairs relief with continued repayment: “payment in an amount equal to 35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2], with interest on the unpaid balance at “50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury” [2].
  • Because Huffman described the result as “a carefully negotiated and narrowly tailored bipartisan bill to support the completion of this project” [5].
  • Because Listening to people with different views includes taking their reasons seriously enough to shape a shared solution.
  • So Enacting these terms turns that listening into payment relief shaped by competing views. [NAME]'s commitment to listening and understanding gives a reason to favor this practical agreement.
points.con_html:
Response Taking opposing reasons seriously does not give tolerance a reason to favor the resulting deal just because it was negotiated.

  • Because Huffman describes concerns about “removing interest payments and extending the repayment period” [5] and says senators “worked to address these shared concerns” [5].
  • Because The bill still requires “payment in an amount equal to 35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2]. For the unpaid balance, subject to financial hardship, it allows “a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury” [2].
  • Because [NAME]'s value favors hearing and understanding people's reasons. It does not favor a particular financial balance just because that balance reflects a compromise. Accepting people and assessing their financial proposals are separate judgments.
  • So The PRO shows how competing views shaped the deal. Enacting it would carry out the agreed financial terms, but their negotiated origin supplies no bridge from valuing a fair hearing to favoring those terms.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Boebert’s drafting credit names the Bureau of Reclamation and the district. Huffman’s “looked past their political differences” refers to House members’ treatment of the bill’s sponsors. The record does not describe how the residents differ from, or disagree with, a given reader. Sources: [3], [5].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect On January 8, 2026, existing law required repayment “within fifty years from the time the works are first available for the delivery of water” [1]. H.R.131 eases repayment of the unpaid balance: “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary, repayment of the balance not covered under subparagraph (A) for a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [2].

points.title: Helping construction continue puts Native cultural ties to ancestral places and burial traditions at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Helping construction continue puts Native cultural ties to ancestral places and burial traditions at risk.

  • Because The current financing creates a stopping point. Water district board president Bill Long explains the bill's importance: “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” [8]
  • Because The project's environmental review identifies prehistoric sites in the area it could affect: “Archaeological resources also include two prehistoric sites.” [9]
  • Because The review also records a tie to living tribes: “PA consulting parties, including all invited Indian Tribes, are as follows” [9], a list that includes the “Comanche Nation” [9].
  • Because The review treats encountering undisturbed historic places as a construction risk. Its route plan aims “to diminish the probability of encountering any undisturbed historic properties.” [9]
  • Because It does not guarantee avoiding every burial: “All known burials or cemeteries will be avoided to the extent possible.” [9]
  • So Easing the financial barrier helps more construction proceed with a remaining risk to ancestral places and graves.
  • Because These places matter to living cultures. The National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers explains: “Connections to cultural heritage sustain the health and vitality of Native peoples.” [10]
  • Because Disturbing graves can violate the beliefs expressed through burial traditions. Southern Ute preservation official Cassandra Atencio explains: “When you put somebody in the ground, you expect them to stay there because you made prayers or did something over them, and that meant something so they could go somewhere else. When you uncover that, you're disturbing them, and now you're bringing them back.” [11]
  • Because Listening to and accepting people with different beliefs gives weight to their cultural ties and burial practices, even when [NAME] does not share those beliefs.
  • So Respecting those practices gives [NAME] a reason to oppose financing that advances this risk of disturbance.
  • Note The objection concerns disturbance itself. The plan requires compliance before work restarts: “only when compliance has been completed.” [9] That cannot undo any disturbance that led to discovering a grave.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect the later construction helped by repayment relief to Native graves. This response does not reach the PRO’s concern for ancestral places more generally.

  • Because The environmental review says, “Archaeological resources also include two prehistoric sites.” [9]
  • Because The original environmental impact statement describes what such recorded sites are: “Prehistoric site types include open camps, open stone tool scatters, kill sites, open architectural, and rock art.” [12] It lists “cemeteries” [12] among historic site types.
  • Because The statement’s surveys are incomplete: “These inventories surveyed between 4 and 19 percent of potential affected area.” [12] So the record does not rule graves out; it also does not show them.
  • Because The burial provision addresses a condition: “If a burial or cemetery cannot be avoided or is encountered during construction” [9].
  • So A rule for handling a possible discovery does not establish that this work reaches a Native grave, and the recorded site types do not supply that step.
  • Because Atencio’s account explains the meaning of uncovering a buried person: “When you uncover that, you're disturbing them, and now you're bringing them back.” [11] It is a general account, not a statement about this project.
  • Because Listening to and accepting people gives weight to their beliefs. It does not turn a general account of burial beliefs into evidence that this work would disturb such a burial.
  • So The grave part of the PRO’s reason needs a link to this work that its sources do not supply.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The EIS reports 850 cultural resources within a 2-mile buffer across all alternatives, including 55 prehistoric sites and 53 prehistoric isolates, and says inventories surveyed between 4 and 19 percent of the potentially affected area. Inventory results and tribal and state consultations could shift alignments to avoid known sites. On federal or trust land Reclamation follows NAGPRA; on state or private land it follows state unmarked burial law and the programmatic agreement. Work stops if unrecorded resources are found. Sources: [12], [9].

Evidence note: Bill Long said existing funds carry construction for another three to five years and that the repayment problem arises in the second half of the project. The record reviewed does not say which recorded sites lie in that half. Sources: [8].

points.title: Helping replace contaminated water protects against cancer, kidney harm and infections.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Helping replace contaminated water protects against cancer, kidney harm and infections.

  • Because Communities the conduit would serve have unsafe water sources: “The drinking water sources they rely on are often contaminated with unsafe levels of radium, uranium, and other pollutants.” [5]

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect H.R.131 eases repayment to help finish the Arkansas Valley Conduit. Existing law requires “35 percent nonfederal repayment over a 50-year period, starting after project completion.” [1] The bill keeps that share: “payment in an amount equal to 35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2]. It counts “funding provided during construction from any entity other than the Secretary” [2] toward payment. For the unpaid balance, it allows “a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [2]. Simple interest charges no interest on past interest. The Interior Department must find hardship: “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2].

  • Because Repayment is a barrier to completion: “the communities that it will serve do not have the financial capacity to meet the traditional repayment obligations.” [3]
  • Because Public resources are already committed: “More than $249 million has already been spent on the AVC” [4].
  • So Lower interest and more years to repay ease that barrier and help bring existing construction into service.

points.title: It helps protect communities from contaminated drinking water.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps protect communities from contaminated drinking water.

  • Because The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation found groundwater with “cancer-causing radioactive contaminants including naturally occurring radium and uranium.” [5]
  • Because On January 8, the House Natural Resources Committee chair reported: “18 of those communities are currently failing to meet Federal drinking water standards due to these contaminants.” [3]
  • Because The finished conduit will deliver clean water to “39 rural communities across southeastern Colorado.” [6]
  • Because Protecting shared drinking water serves societal security. The federal plan for water security calls the water sector “a lifeline sector” [7] and states: “Safe drinking water is a prerequisite for protecting public health and all human activity” [7].
  • So Helping finish a shared safe-water system strengthens the government's ability to defend U.S. communities against a documented health threat. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a country that protects its citizens.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: Sources differ on key counts. Reclamation’s ROD and 2024 testimony refer to twelve providers under orders or exceeding standards, while the chair and the district refer to 18. Municipal Sewer & Water reports about 39,000 residents in the 39 communities, while most sources say about 50,000. Sources: [5], [10], [3], [11].

points.title: It helps secure enough water to keep communities and essential services running.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps secure enough water to keep communities and essential services running.

  • Because Some local sources run short: “springs that supply some of the underground water sources can dry up periodically.” [11]
  • Because The conduit supplies water from elsewhere: “It will transport water that originates in the Fryingpan River basin on the western slope of the Continental Divide” [11]. Reclamation says it will “help meet existing and future municipal and industrial water demands” [5].
  • Because The services supplied include “water for hospitals in towns such as La Junta” [12] and “water for rural schools in communities such as Lamar” [12].
  • Because Water shortages threaten services beyond household drinking needs. The federal plan for water security identifies “fire protection, healthcare, and heating and cooling processes” [7] as critical services disrupted by interrupted water service.
  • So Easier financing helps meet water needs despite local shortages and future demand. Keeping communities, schools, and hospitals supplied supports the United States' ability to protect people and maintain stable daily life.

The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: The 2022 EA states that the project would not increase Fryingpan-Arkansas Project water diversions. The conduit delivers water by pipe rather than adding river diversions. Sources: [13].

points.title: It strengthens water providers' ability to sustain an essential public service.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It strengthens water providers' ability to sustain an essential public service.

  • Because Local providers face tight budgets: “Rural water providers in our area often struggle to secure the funding needed to meet the needs of the communities they serve.” [14]
  • Because The parties paying for the conduit must also keep it working. The bill requires “the assumption by the contracting parties of the care, operation, maintenance, and replacement of the conduit.” [2]
  • Because County commissioners say completing the conduit would “help reduce the financial burden on these providers and enhance their ability to deliver a higher quality and a more reliable water supply” [14].
  • So Reducing the yearly repayment burden makes the shared supply more affordable for strained providers. Helping them sustain water service strengthens the public capacity needed to protect citizens.

Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: Secondary accounts describe the bill’s hardship clause differently from its text. The district’s post-veto message says it “Provides an opportunity for a federal decision on debt forgiveness based on economic hardship,” and the Colorado Sun says it may have allowed Reclamation to forgive some loan payments. The bill text ties a term of up to 75 years at half the Treasury rate to a demonstration of financial hardship and does not use the word forgiveness. Sources: [8], [15], [2].

points.title: It helps protect the pipes and equipment that keep water flowing.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It helps protect the pipes and equipment that keep water flowing.

  • Because Dissolved minerals in existing supplies cause physical damage. Reclamation found “corrosion and scaling effects that lead to premature deterioration of distribution pipes, water treatment equipment” [5].
  • Because Its updated assessment retains the conduit's benefits from “reducing total dissolved solids concentrations” [13], meaning less dissolved mineral material in supplied water.
  • So Helping deliver less damaging water slows wear on essential water systems. Preserving those systems strengthens the United States' ability to maintain services its communities depend on.

The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It helps protect a shared river from polluted treatment waste.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It helps protect a shared river from polluted treatment waste.

  • Because In Las Animas, treating polluted well water creates another problem. The water district's president described “contaminated waste water that is a byproduct of treatment.” [16] He said: “We can discharge that back to the river, but we can’t do that in perpetuity.” [16]
  • Because That waste poses a pollution risk to a shared river: “the Arkansas River’s own water quality problems, which can be worsened by the discharges.” [16]
  • Because Reclamation says the conduit will “supplement or replace existing poor-quality groundwater sources” [13].
  • So Replacing polluted well water reduces the need for the local treatment that produces this waste. Helping finance that change protects a shared U.S. water resource from this source of pollution. Protecting essential water resources serves [NAME]'s concern for a secure country.

The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: The district president said the state will not allow Las Animas to discharge indefinitely. The 2013 EIS assumed zero liquid discharge under all alternatives. La Junta is seeking grants to reduce concentrate volume. The timing of any requirement is not stated in the record. Sources: [16], [17], [18].

points.title: It helps rural communities maintain viable local economies.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It helps rural communities maintain viable local economies.

  • Because The region faces “low income, and its shrinking population and economy” [16].
  • Because Existing water limits business activity. The water district's president explained: “If we try to do anything in Las Animas that requires a new water supply, we can’t do it.” [16]
  • Because Reclamation's experience with other rural water projects supports the link to stability: when clean water becomes available, “businesses can turn their attention to new opportunities” [5] and “communities can gain stability” [5].
  • Because These communities also house food producers: they “support families who ranch and raise livestock.” [3]
  • So Helping finance a usable new supply removes a water barrier to business activity and supports viable towns, including ranching communities. Sustaining U.S. communities directly serves [NAME]'s concern for a stable country.

The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.131 lowers interest and allows longer repayment on the conduit’s unpaid local construction share. Existing law provides “35 percent nonfederal repayment over a 50-year period” [1]. For the balance left after contributions during construction, the bill allows “a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [2], “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2].

points.title: The added financing cost draws on federal resources available for defense and emergencies.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The added financing cost draws on federal resources available for defense and emergencies.

  • Because The existing interest rate is tied to Treasury’s borrowing costs: “computed average interest rate payable by the Treasury upon its outstanding marketable public obligations” [1].
  • Because Receiving the same payment later is worth less. CBO explains that “an amount received or paid today is more valuable than the same amount received or paid in the future.” [19]
  • Because CBO’s July 2025 table lists the bill’s effect on direct spending as “Increase by Less Than $500K” [20].
  • So The cheaper financing adds a federal cost. Keeping the current terms preserves the federal resources that cover it.
  • Because Federal financing costs compete with defense spending. A report by the Joint Economic Committee’s chair states: “Interest costs use revenue that could be used for other government outlays, such as national defense.” [21]
  • Because CBO identifies “respond to unforeseen events” [22] as another purpose of federal tax and spending policy.
  • Because [NAME] values a state with the means to defend its citizens and protect them against new threats.
  • So Preserving funds available for defense and emergency action serves that value and gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added subsidy.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats higher promised repayments as funds that keeping the current terms would preserve, but the record reports a payment problem under those terms. This response does not dispute that CBO lists a small direct-spending increase, and it does not reach the PRO’s reasoning from a federal cost to resources for other uses.

  • Because The bill makes the easier repayment terms depend on hardship: “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2].
  • Because In 2024 testimony on an earlier bill, the repayment district assessed whether income from contracts to use project facilities could cover its share after construction costs rose: “Repayment can now be accomplished only if the interest rate is reduced to at least half the current project rate and the repayment period is at least 75 years, 25 years longer than the currently authorized 50 years.” [23]
  • Because Reclamation confirmed the payment problem under the existing law: “Given this increase, the project beneficiaries are again faced with challenges to repay their share of construction of the project, as directed under P.L. 111-11.” [10]
  • Because The PRO’s own CBO source accounts for missed payments when valuing loans. It describes “the expected cost of default, which CBO accounts for in projected cash flows rather than in the discount rate.” [19]
  • So An interest rate tied to federal borrowing costs and an earlier due date set what is owed. They do not show what would be collected. Comparing the value of the promised payments leaves out the payment problem. The PRO has not shown that keeping the old terms preserves the higher repayments it counts as available funds.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Secondary accounts describe the bill’s hardship clause differently from its text. The district’s post-veto message says it “Provides an opportunity for a federal decision on debt forgiveness based on economic hardship,” and the Colorado Sun says it may have allowed Reclamation to forgive some loan payments. The bill text ties a term of up to 75 years at half the Treasury rate to a demonstration of financial hardship and does not use the word forgiveness. Sources: [8], [15], [2].

Evidence note: The bill’s only cost figure in the record is CBO’s July 2025 listing of “Increase by Less Than $500K” in direct spending and no effect on revenues, in a table CBO says was prepared with limited review time. Sponsors say the bill “does not authorize any additional Federal funding.” The JEC and CBO statements cited concern the national debt in general. The JEC statement concerns net interest on the national debt, and the CBO statement concerns deficit-financed policy under a large debt. Neither names a program this bill would reduce. Sources: [20], [21], [3].

statements: to maintain traditional values and ways of thinking
to follow their family's customs or the customs of a religion

pages.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
pages.description: H.R.131 would have reduced what communities in Colorado must repay the federal government for building the Arkansas Valley Conduit, a federal water pipeline. It would have lowered the interest they owe and extended their repayment period.
