directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, H.R.131 would ease repayment for the existing drinking-water pipeline. Current law requires repayment “within fifty years from the time the works are first available for the delivery of water” [1]. For the balance left after funding provided during construction, the bill requires “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2] and allows “a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [2]. The required share stays at “35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2]. These terms help make completion affordable: the local water district's board president explains, “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” [3]

points.title: Helping deliver safe water follows the Christian duties to serve the thirsty and protect life.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Helping deliver safe water follows the Christian duties to serve the thirsty and protect life.

  • Because Communities awaiting the pipeline face a health threat: “The drinking water sources they rely on are often contaminated with unsafe levels of radium, uranium, and other pollutants.” [4]
  • Because Jesus's teaching praises giving water to those in need: “I was thirsty and you gave Me drink.” [5]
  • Because The Baptist Faith and Message calls Christians to “contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death.” [6]
  • Because Evangelical teaching also applies water provision to public action. The National Association of Evangelicals says, “We urge governments” [7] to “provide safe drinking water” [7].
  • So Helping finance a safer water supply puts those inherited teachings into practice through public policy. [NAME]'s wish to follow Christian tradition therefore supports this relief.
points.con_html:
Response The personal service the PRO invokes is not carried out by supporting public loan terms. This response does not answer the PRO’s separate appeal to the National Association of Evangelicals’ public-policy call.

  • Because The family following Jesus’s teaching describes its service as “giving and sacrificing our time and resources” [5]. Christian writer Robert Sirico distinguishes public aid from that duty: “What is required of us as individuals may or may not translate into a civic policy priority.” [8] He adds: “a government program effects nothing toward fulfilling the Gospel requirement that we give of our own time and income toward assisting the poor.” [8]
  • Because The National Association of Evangelicals calls on governments to “provide safe drinking water” [7]. That is a public-policy goal, separate from the personal giving in the passage the PRO quotes.
  • So The “thirsty” teaching and the personal duty to serve do not by themselves make favoring these terms an inherited Christian practice. That step needs the public-policy teaching and not the duty of personal service.
points.retirement_reason: Safe water and care for people are the substantive goals. Religious support for those goals does not independently establish Tradition fit.

points.title: Affordable water can help sustain the town where a Christmas caroling tradition continues.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Affordable water can help sustain the town where a Christmas caroling tradition continues.

  • Because Unsafe water “forces many families to rely on bottled water or expensive filtration systems” [4]. H.R.131 addresses local affordability by “cutting local costs by lowering the interest rate and providing more flexible repayment terms.” [9]
  • Because The district's spokesman identifies water quality as a barrier to living in valley towns: “It's a great lifestyle and one of the big drawbacks is the water quality.” [10]
  • So Easing the cost of a safer supply supports the households and towns where these families can keep living.
  • Because The district lists “Town of Swink” [12] among conduit participants. Its church keeps a shared religious custom: “The Swink United Methodists Shared Their Annual Tradition of Christmas Caroling with the Community.” [13]
  • So By easing a stated cost and water-quality barrier to remaining in these towns, the bill can help sustain the community in which this annual Christmas caroling custom is practiced. Continuing that named religious custom, rather than water quality alone, supplies the Tradition connection.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The same district spokesman passage says “the decline of a lot of the communities in the Lower Arkansas Valley is directly related to the poor quality of water.” The farm article’s stated water threat concerns irrigation water being purchased and diverted, which the bill does not address. Sources: [10], [14].

points.title: Hardship relief follows Christian mercy toward borrowers while helping communities meet their repayment duties.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Hardship relief follows Christian mercy toward borrowers while helping communities meet their repayment duties.

  • Because The difficulty is an inability to pay: “the communities that it will serve do not have the financial capacity to meet the traditional repayment obligations.” [4]
  • Because The bill ties easier repayment to “a demonstration of financial hardship” [2] for a project serving “communities and households that do not have reliable access to domestic water supplies” [2].
  • Because Kevin DeYoung's account of Christian lending judges loans by their effect on borrowers: “It depends on whether the loan will help the borrower or most likely hurt them.” [16]
  • Because Christian concern for people in need is an express duty: “We should work to provide for the orphaned, the needy, the abused, the aged, the helpless, and the sick.” [6]
  • Because Repayment is also a Christian duty in public finance. Joe Carter explains that elected representatives take on “contractual debt obligations” [17] and concludes, “For this reason, I believe as Christians we should not refuse to pay for the legal obligations that we have authorized.” [17]
  • So A lower rate and more time make repayment fit hardship while retaining the required share. [NAME] can honor both mercy toward borrowers in need and responsibility for paying debts by favoring these terms.
points.con_html:
Response DeYoung’s help-or-hurt test sets loans for urgent personal needs apart from other lending, so it does not establish that mercy toward borrowers covers this water district’s construction debt. This response does not reach the PRO’s separate appeal to repayment duty.

  • Because DeYoung’s test concerns which loans count as usury. He explains, “But not every sort of interest-bearing loan has been considered usury.” [16] He distinguishes loans for urgent personal needs from another kind: “But a loan as a business venture or investment risk has historically been considered a different kind of loan.” [16]
  • Because The bill requires “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. That condition concerns the project’s financing, not a loan for a person’s urgent needs.
  • Because The broader duty is addressed to Christians: “We should work to provide for the orphaned, the needy, the abused, the aged, the helpless, and the sick.” [6] It does not say that easing a public project’s debt is how that duty is carried out.
  • So The PRO’s sources do not establish that easing this public construction debt falls within the mercy they describe. Its appeal to repayment duty is not answered here.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: DeYoung’s article describes Old Testament loans as given to the destitute and says that in such cases one must not charge interest, while distinguishing loans of capital. The article does not discuss public water-project repayment. Carter says an individual must pay “to the best of their ability” and writes about the debt ceiling. H.R.131 keeps the 35 percent share while changing the rate and the deadline. Sources: [16], [17].
points.retirement_reason: Mercy in public debt terms is a general moral justification, without a particular inherited debt observance or practice affected by the bill.

points.title: Making the longstanding federal water pledge workable honors the Christian duty to keep one's word.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Making the longstanding federal water pledge workable honors the Christian duty to keep one's word.

  • Because The commitment reaches back generations: “Over six decades ago, President John Kennedy came to Pueblo, CO, and famously promised to build the Arkansas Valley Conduit.” [9]
  • Because Financing relief helps carry out that pledge: “it would fulfill a decades--many decades--old promise on which they have relied.” [9]
  • Because Christian teaching treats promises as binding: “Jesus here stresses that the word of a Christian should be such that a “yes” or a “no” carries binding force.” [18]
  • Because That moral standard can guide public conduct. The Baptist Faith and Message says, “Every Christian should seek to bring industry, government, and society as a whole under the sway of the principles of righteousness, truth, and brotherly love.” [6]
  • So Favoring terms that help the government carry out its pledge lets [NAME] uphold an inherited moral standard in public life.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The 1962 Act authorized the project and made a repayment contract a condition precedent to construction. Congress reduced the conduit’s required share to 35 percent in 2009. Reclamation’s 2024 testimony says completing the conduit “fulfills a commitment the federal government made decades ago.” H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. The 1962 repayment clause runs “as rapidly as is consistent with the contracting parties' ability to pay, but in any event, within fifty years.” Senator Bennet says Kennedy “famously promised to build” the conduit, and the Project Management Plan says completion “will fulfill a project authorization from 1962.” The text of the 1962 Pueblo address is not in the record. Sources: [19], [20], [1], [9], [21].
points.retirement_reason: Keeping a public commitment is the substantive justification; invoking an inherited promise does not turn ordinary promise-keeping into Tradition.

points.title: Helping turn existing construction into a working water supply follows Christian stewardship.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Helping turn existing construction into a working water supply follows Christian stewardship.

  • Because Public resources are already committed: “More than $249 million has already been spent on the AVC” [22].
  • Because Completing the project gives that work a useful purpose: “Once completed, the Arkansas Valley Conduit will deliver clean water to over 50,000 people in 39 rural communities across southeastern Colorado.” [9]
  • Because Christian stewardship means using what God entrusts to people well: “A thoughtful stewardship of all that we have is part of our Christian discipleship.” [23] Its purpose includes others' welfare: “We, in turn, are thus responsible for using his blessings for his glory, our benefit and the welfare of others.” [23]
  • So By easing the repayment obstacle to completion, the bill helps put existing work and public money to their intended use. [NAME] can favor that productive use of resources as an expression of inherited Christian stewardship.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The 1962 Act authorized the project and made a repayment contract a condition precedent to construction. Congress reduced the conduit’s required share to 35 percent in 2009. Reclamation’s 2024 testimony says completing the conduit “fulfills a commitment the federal government made decades ago.” H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. The 1962 repayment clause runs “as rapidly as is consistent with the contracting parties' ability to pay, but in any event, within fifty years.” Senator Bennet says Kennedy “famously promised to build” the conduit, and the Project Management Plan says completion “will fulfill a project authorization from 1962.” The text of the 1962 Pueblo address is not in the record. Sources: [19], [20], [1], [9], [21].

Evidence note: The veto message reports “More than $249 million has already been spent on the AVC” and “total costs are estimated to be $1.3 billion,” so the larger part of the estimated cost lies ahead. H.R.131 appropriates none of it. The stewardship source speaks of personal resources. Sources: [22], [23].
points.retirement_reason: Productive spending and stewardship are general prudential duties here, not an identified inherited practice or way of life.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.131?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill keeps the construction repayment share at “35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2]. For the balance after construction contributions, relief is “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. Repayment can last “not more than 75 years” [2] at “50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” [2]. The law in force on January 8, 2026 requires repayment “within fifty years from the time the works are first available for the delivery of water” [1]. Its full interest rate rests on “the computed average interest rate payable by the Treasury upon its outstanding marketable public obligations” [1].

points.title: The interest discount shifts financing costs from users to the public, against the inherited Christian ethic of responsibility and thrift.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The interest discount shifts financing costs from users to the public, against the inherited Christian ethic of responsibility and thrift.

  • Because This is public financing: existing law provides “100 percent federal construction financing” [1].
  • So For the same unpaid balance and time, users would owe half the interest charged at the existing benchmark. The public supplies that financing discount.
  • Because Chuck Colson links responsibility to Christian heritage: “As heirs to the Christian work ethic, we Americans value liberty and self-reliance. Hard work. Paying our bills. Delaying our gratification.” [24]
  • Because Colson applies restraint to public finances: “It's a moral issue. Living within our means, caring about our children and grandchildren, saving our society.” [24]
  • Because Concerned Women for America calls for a return to “historically-proven, time-honored principles” [25], including “individual freedom and responsibility” [25].
  • Because Writing about government loan relief, Jeremiah Greever applies Christian teaching directly to public lending: “he doesn’t call us to lend someone else’s money and then change the terms of the lending agreement.” [26]
  • So Keeping this inherited ethic in public lending gives [NAME] a reason to oppose shifting more of users’ financing costs to the public.
  • Note The sponsor says the bill “does not authorize any additional Federal funding” [4]. The objection concerns the discounted price of public lending, which the bill changes.
points.con_html:
Response An interest discount on public lending does not establish the failure of responsibility the PRO infers from it. This response does not answer Greever’s separate objection to changing the terms of a loan made with others’ money.

  • Because Existing law requires “payment in an amount equal to 35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [1]. The bill keeps “35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2] and assigns the contracting parties “the care, operation, maintenance, and replacement of the conduit.” [2]
  • Because Crown explains the repayment teaching this way: “The implication of this Scripture is that the wicked can repay but will not, as opposed to those who want to repay but cannot.” [27]
  • Because Focus on the Family publishes Crown’s advice that borrowers unable to make minimum payments ask creditors to “reduce the interest and/or accept what you can afford to pay.” [28] It adds, “If they accept your proposal, pay that amount faithfully until it is totally repaid.” [28]
  • So In this teaching, lower interest can be part of faithful repayment. A hardship discount does not itself show that borrowers are shirking their duties.
  • Because Colson’s account of Christian responsibility also recognizes government, family, church and business as institutions that “all have vital and proper roles to play in society, balancing each other.” [24]
  • Because The National Association of Evangelicals’ civic platform urges governments to “provide safe drinking water” [7]. Existing law requires evidence that “it would be infeasible for the communities involved to construct the works themselves, singly or jointly.” [1]
  • So The work ethic does not settle how the cost of this government task should be shared. The PRO’s general appeals to self-reliance supply no further reason why the old interest charge better reflects Christian responsibility in this hardship case.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO’s July 2025 listing shows direct spending “Increase by Less Than $500K.” Colson, Perkins and CWA wrote about national spending and debt, not this contract. Sources: [29], [30].
points.retirement_reason: The objection is fiscal prudence or responsibility to descendants; religious endorsement alone does not establish a distinct Tradition stake.

points.title: The longer repayment limit permits debt to bind later generations, against Christian teaching to limit long-term debt and provide for descendants.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The longer repayment limit permits debt to bind later generations, against Christian teaching to limit long-term debt and provide for descendants.

  • Because The bill lifts the repayment limit by 25 years. The committee describes “increasing the repayment period from 50 years to 75 years” [1].
  • So Repayment claims could remain in years 51–75, after the existing legal deadline.
  • Because Albert Mohler identifies the inherited teaching: “The Christian tradition has been very suspicious of credit and borrowing.” [31]
  • Because Crown Financial Ministries makes the rule about duration explicit: “Do not accumulate long-term debt” [27].
  • Because Focus on the Family warns that borrowing reaches into an uncertain future: “it does warn us against making assumptions about the future” [32].
  • Because Family Research Council president Tony Perkins applies biblical money teachings “both as individuals and collectively as communities and countries” [30].
  • Because Perkins grounds his warning about passing public debt to descendants in Proverbs: “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children” [30].
  • So Allowing repayment claims for another 25 years puts later generations’ resources within reach of the debt. Maintaining Christian caution about long commitments and the duty to provide for descendants gives [NAME] a reason to oppose lifting the limit.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that a longer hardship repayment plan falls under its sources’ warnings against accumulating debt and passing overspending to descendants.

  • Because The bill keeps the construction share at “35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2]. Extra time depends on “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. The committee reports that inflation caused project costs “to nearly double from $640 million to $1.3 billion.” [1]
  • Because Crown’s rule, “Do not accumulate long-term debt” [27], discusses lengthening home loans through “expansion through taking on debt” [27]. Perkins warns about “continuing to amass trillions of dollars in debt, debt that is going to be passed to future generations.” [30]
  • Because The same Crown ministry advises hardship borrowers to seek payments they can afford and says, “If they accept your proposal, pay that amount faithfully until it is totally repaid.” [28]
  • Because Mohler’s historical account says, “Usury laws and a bias against borrowing and lending dissuaded most Christians from borrowing except in a dire emergency.” [31] This project addresses unsafe water: Chairman Westerman reported that “18 of those communities are currently failing to meet Federal drinking water standards due to these contaminants.” [4]
  • Because Focus on the Family says, “Sometimes we must take on debt so that we can care for our loved ones.” [32] Its repayment standard is “a moral obligation to repay his or her creditors to the best of their ability.” [32]
  • So These teachings distinguish taking on debt from handling a repayment hardship, and require attention to essential needs and ability to pay. The extra time addresses repayment of the existing construction share. Payments reaching years 51–75 do not by themselves show the debt accumulation or passing on of overspending the PRO’s examples condemn. The PRO supplies no further link from that longer window to neglect of descendants.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Crown’s text states that the longest term of debt God’s people took on in the Bible was about seven years, and criticizes 30-year and longer home loans. It addresses household mortgages. Sources: [27].

Evidence note: CBO’s July 2025 listing shows direct spending “Increase by Less Than $500K.” Colson, Perkins and CWA wrote about national spending and debt, not this contract. Sources: [29], [30].
points.retirement_reason: The objection is fiscal prudence or responsibility to descendants; religious endorsement alone does not establish a distinct Tradition stake.

points.title: The bill gives one conduit special hardship terms, against the biblical rule of impartial government.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill gives one conduit special hardship terms, against the biblical rule of impartial government.

  • Because Existing law already adjusts repayment speed to need: “as rapidly as is consistent with the contracting parties' ability to pay” [1]. It still imposes the 50-year deadline quoted above.
  • Because The act’s ordinary interest rule covers water supplied to towns and homes: “municipal, domestic, and industrial water supply allocations” [1]. Its ordinary cost-recovery rule requires repayment “within not more than fifty years” [1].
  • Because The bill gives the discounted rate and longer term specifically to “the contract for the Arkansas Valley Conduit” [2], “notwithstanding the reclamation laws or any other provision of this Act” [2].
  • So Hardship in this conduit qualifies for half its applicable Treasury benchmark and up to 75 years. Other hardship cases under the act would still face its ordinary full benchmark and 50-year limit.
  • Because WORLD’s biblical account of government calls for “public impartiality” [33] and says “extra sensitivity to abuse of the poor does not warrant prejudice in their favor” [33].
  • So Applying this inherited rule to public lending calls for common rules for hardship. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose an exception whose relief also depends on which project a community uses.
points.con_html:
Response Project-specific hardship terms do not by themselves establish the favoritism barred by the cited teaching.

  • Because WORLD says, “In this way godly justice and righteousness focus on process.” [33] Its rule is to “judge your neighbor fairly” [33].
  • Because The bill bases relief on “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. The committee identifies a concrete repayment problem: inflation caused costs “to nearly double from $640 million to $1.3 billion.” [1]
  • So The exception has a reason tied to repayment capacity. Its project-specific scope alone does not show the biased judgment WORLD condemns.
  • So The PRO compares legal deadlines and rates, but supplies no comparison showing the same repayment capacity, cost increases, and water-access problems. Sharing a legal deadline does not establish the same financial need. The rule against favoritism therefore does not establish that these different hardship terms treat comparable cases unfairly.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Reclamation testified that the conduit is “unique within Reclamation’s authorized projects” in keeping repayment of a large upfront cost while serving only municipal and industrial purposes. GAO reported in 1996 that reclamation law does not require irrigators to pay interest on repayment obligations. Sources: [20], [34].
points.retirement_reason: Impartial treatment in repayment is a justice concern. Its religious endorsement does not establish preservation of a particular tradition.
